events.text: You wake before the roosters to a sound like a hundred doors closing at once, far away. At first light the whole town is in the street, looking up. On the hill where yesterday there were only pines and a goat path, a pagoda stands, roof upon roof upon roof, so many that the top is lost in the haze. Nobody heard it built. The goats are grazing at its foot as if it had always been there.

choices.text: Climb the goat path and see it up close

effects.log: Up close it is older than it looked: the wood worn silver, the steps hollowed by feet that cannot have climbed them, for it was not here yesterday. The doors are shut. No lock, no bar, no handle. Only dust on the first step, and in the dust no footprint but yours.

choices.text: Count the roofs from the town square

effects.log: You lose your place twice. The third time you reach a hundred and stop, because the last roof has a shape you have no word for, and looking at it too long makes your eyes water.

choices.text: Close the shutters. It is none of your business

effects.log: You go back to bed and do not sleep. All morning a thin line of its shadow lies across your room, though the sun is on the other side of the house.

events.text: It rains for three days without stopping. When the clouds lift, there is a pagoda on the hill above the town, its eaves still dripping, a bell hanging still and silent at every corner of every roof. A carter who drove the hill road at midnight swears he passed nothing but pines and rain. At dawn he drove back the same way, and his mule would not walk past the new steps for any whip.

choices.text: Buy the carter a drink and hear it all

effects.log: He tells it three times, and it is the same each time, which is what frightens him. "The mule knew," he says. "The mule bowed its head, like at a grave."

choices.text: Lead the mule past the steps yourself

effects.log: The mule plants its feet. You coax it, pull it, and at last it walks past with its eyes shut, trembling. On the far side it shakes itself like a wet dog and will not look back.

choices.text: Light incense at its foot, as the old women do

effects.log: The smoke goes straight up along the doors, as if drawn, and does not drift. The old women nod at each other as though that settles something.

events.text: The market sells nothing today but talk. Overnight a pagoda of a hundred roofs has stood up on the hill above the town, and every trader has a theory: a sect's secret vault, a forgotten tomb, a demon's lantern, a joke of Heaven's. The fishwife says only that at moonset the hill was bare, because she was watching it, because she could not sleep.

choices.text: Listen to every theory, and believe none of them

effects.log: By evening you have heard forty answers. None of them explains why the pagoda's many bells hang so still in the wind that is bending the market awnings.

choices.text: Sell the crowd a "true account" for a copper each

effects.log: Your account is mostly invention and sells very well. That night you dream of a door, and in the dream it is disappointed in you.

choices.text: Ask the fishwife what she saw

effects.log: "Nothing," she says. "That is what I keep telling them. Bare hill, moon going down. Then I blinked. You do not get a hundred roofs in a blink. Unless they were always there and we were the ones not looking."

events.text: In a single season four great sects send scouts to the hill. They camp at the pagoda's foot in four camps that do not speak to each other. The orthodox scouts try courtesy and bow at the doors for nine days. The demonic scouts try crowbars. By the first frost every camp is gone, and every report sent home says the same thing in different words: it does not open.

choices.text: Bring the scouts tea and hear what they will not write

effects.log: An old scout warms his hands on the cup. "Twelve years I have opened things for my sect," he says. "Tombs. Vaults. A dead emperor's privy. This is the first door I ever tried that felt like it was trying me back."

choices.text: Shadow the scouts and read their reports

effects.log: You read them by candlelight in an empty inn. Four sects, four styles of handwriting, one shared confession at the end of each: "We do not know what it is."

choices.text: Sit on the steps after they have all gone

effects.log: The hill is quiet. Your breathing slows to the pace of something much older than you. When you stand, the sun has moved a long way and you do not remember it moving.

events.text: A huge man of the unorthodox path comes up the hill with an iron hammer the size of a millstone, says he has never met a door he could not open, and swings. The door does not mark. The hammer rings like a bell, one long clean note that goes on after he has let go of it. He stands listening until it stops. Then he walks down the hill without a word, leaving the hammer on the step.

choices.text: Run after him and ask what he heard

effects.log: He does not slow down. "My name," he says at last. "It said my name. Not loudly. The way you say the name of someone you are going to see later."

choices.text: Lift the hammer he left behind

effects.log: It takes everything you have to lift one end. When you set it down, the step under it has not a scratch, and a little dust has already settled over the place it lay.

choices.text: Keep well away from anything that rings like that

effects.log: You go home the long way round. Some sounds are not meant for you, and you have lived this long by knowing which.

events.text: A famous swordsman of the Heavenly Rankings comes to cut the doors at noon, before half the province. It is a perfect cut; people talk about it for years. The edge goes into the wood the way a hand goes into water, and comes out clean, and there is no mark. Afterwards, white in the face, the swordsman says only: "It was like cutting a question. And the question was not for me."

choices.text: Ask the swordsman what that means

effects.log: "I do not know," the swordsman says. "That is what I mean." And then, more quietly: "I think it was waiting for someone who does not need a sword to ask it."

choices.text: Go up after the crowd leaves and look for the cut

effects.log: There is no cut. There is a faint warmth in the wood where the edge went in, the warmth of a hand that has just let go, and then not even that.

choices.text: Cheer with the crowd. It was a fine cut

effects.log: It was a fine cut. The pagoda did not seem to mind it, the way a mountain does not mind the wind.

events.text: There is no wind tonight. Not a leaf moves, the lamp flame stands up straight as a needle, and every dog in the town is lying flat with its ears back. Then, from the hill, a bell. One stroke: a deep, plain, patient sound. It does not come from the bells at the eaves; those hang still. It comes from inside.

choices.text: Run up the hill in the dark

effects.log: You fall twice on the goat path. At the top the doors are shut and silent. But the bronze bell above them, at the lowest eave, is warm under your fingers, as if it has only just stopped wanting to ring.

choices.text: Wait by the window for a second stroke

effects.log: It never comes. You wait until the sky greys. By then you are sure, without knowing how, that the bell was not rung for you. It was rung because someone, somewhere, had done something worth one stroke.

choices.text: Bar the door and pull the quilt over your head

effects.log: The sound stays in the house all night anyway, not loud, just there, like a guest who has decided to be patient.

events.text: Two old monks of the hill temple have been arguing about the pagoda for a month: in the courtyard, at meals, in their sleep. Elder Hyeon-gak says it is a curse, for a thing that comes without being built has no right to stand. Elder Do-un says it is an omen, for nothing evil would trouble itself to hang so many bells. The novices have taken sides. Both old men stop you in the street and ask which of them is right.

choices.text: "A curse. Nothing honest arrives overnight."

effects.log: Hyeon-gak nods grimly and Do-un looks at you with great sorrow. That night the novices of the curse side find the temple bell will not sound for them, and nobody can say why.

choices.text: "An omen. Something is coming, and it is not cruel."

effects.log: Do-un beams. Hyeon-gak mutters that omens are only curses with good manners. For a week the temple is full of people come to look up the hill.

choices.text: Ask each of them what they are really afraid of

effects.log: Hyeon-gak is afraid it is for somebody else. Do-un is afraid it is for him, and that he is too old. They look at each other a long time, and go back up to the temple together, not arguing.

events.text: The beggar under the bridge has a story and will tell it for a copper. On the night of the new moon he saw a light on the hundredth roof. "Not a lamp," he says. "Lamps flicker. This did not flicker. It was the colour the sky goes before there is any sun, and it was in the shape of a door." He has told it to a hundred people and nobody believes him. He does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Give him silver and ask what else he saw

effects.log: He leans in close. "It was shut," he says. "But it was there. Up top, where there is nothing to stand on. A door does not get put where nobody can reach it, does it? Not unless someone is supposed to."

choices.text: Watch the highest roof yourself on the next new moon

effects.log: You sit up all night in the cold. Near dawn, for the length of one breath, you think you see it: a pale edge, like light under a door. Then the sun comes and you cannot be sure of anything.

choices.text: Laugh, and toss him a copper anyway

effects.log: He laughs too, cheerfully. "They all laugh," he says. "Then they look up. You will look up."

events.text: A travelling bell-caster from the south stands under the pagoda's eaves all afternoon with her head tipped back. At last she says the bronze is funeral bronze, the kind a village casts for its dead, and that whoever cast it knew the trade better than anyone now living. Then she counts the bells twice and frowns. Every eave has its bell, but one. The highest hook is empty.

choices.text: Help her measure the bronze

effects.log: She pays you a little for holding the cord. "The clappers are tied," she says, pointing. "Every one, with red thread. Someone is keeping them quiet until it is time."

choices.text: Ask what kind of person casts bells for the dead

effects.log: She is quiet for a while. "Someone who could not do anything else for them," she says. "You cast the bell because you could not keep the person. I have always thought that is the saddest trade there is, and the best."

choices.text: Buy her a meal and hear about her trade

effects.log: Over noodles she tells you of furnaces and clay moulds, of the first bell she ever cast, which cracked. "Whoever cast those," she says, nodding at the hill, "cast their first one young. You can hear it in the later ones. They never stopped trying to get it right."

events.text: You dream of the pagoda, but it is not the pagoda. It is a spire of grey stone, plain as a fist, on a cold headland over a sea you have never seen, under a sky of a colour you have no word for. There is a lamp in one high window. When you wake, the real pagoda stands on its hill in the dawn as always, and for a moment you could swear the two are the same building, seen from either end.

choices.text: Write the dream down before it fades

effects.log: By the time the ink is dry, half of it is gone. What stays is the cold of the stone, and the lamp, and the feeling that someone behind it had been waiting a very long time.

choices.text: Tell the monks of the hill temple

effects.log: Elder Do-un listens to the end, then says nothing for so long that you think he has fallen asleep. "Grey stone," he says at last. "Yes. I have had that dream too. Do not tell Hyeon-gak."

choices.text: Put it out of your mind and train

effects.log: You train hard all day. Your mind stays on the work. Only once, resting, you look west and find you are listening for the sea.

events.text: Every morning the pagoda's steps are swept. Nobody in the town has ever seen who does it. Leaves blown up there in the night are gone by dawn; mud from the scouts' boots was gone by dawn. A carter's boy sat up a whole night to catch the sweeper and swears he never closed his eyes, and that all he heard, just before first light, was a broom.

choices.text: Keep watch on the steps yourself

effects.log: You sit up all night in the cold and see no one. At first light the steps are clean, and on the lowest one stands a little cup of barley tea, long cold, as if it had been poured for someone hours ago and they had not come.

choices.text: Leave a coin on the step as thanks

effects.log: The next morning the coin is still there, swept neatly to one side of the step, the dust around it brushed into a careful circle, the way you would leave a gift you were too polite to refuse.

choices.text: Let whoever it is keep their own business

effects.log: Some work is done better unwatched. Still, after that, you hear brooms differently.

events.text: The tester from the sects came through the town this spring and found no spiritual root at all in the potter's youngest child. Since then the child has taken to sitting at the pagoda's foot every evening. "It hums," the child tells you, "when I am sad. Like it is listening." Nobody else has ever heard it hum.

choices.text: Sit down beside the child and listen

effects.log: For a long time, nothing. Then, so low you feel it in your teeth more than hear it, a hum, like a bell remembering being struck. The child looks up at you as if to say: see?

choices.text: Teach the child one breath of the method, root or no root

effects.log: The breath does nothing for the child's body; it cannot. But the child sits straighter after, and the next evening says the hum was louder, "like it liked that."

choices.text: Walk the child home before dark

effects.log: On the way down the child keeps looking back. "It is not for the gifted," the child says suddenly, with great certainty. "I can tell. It is for people like me." You do not know how to answer that.

events.text: At noon a building's shadow should lie in a puddle at its feet. The pagoda's does not. At every hour of the day, in every season, it lies long and thin across the hill, pointing west. Scholars have come from the capital to measure it. They have filled three books and agree on nothing but the direction.

choices.text: Follow the shadow's line west for a day

effects.log: You walk until sunset along the line it points, over fields and a river ford, and find nothing but more west. At dusk, looking back, you see the pagoda small on its hill, and its shadow pointing past you, further still.

choices.text: Help the scholars measure it

effects.log: You hold the rods while they argue. The shadow is exactly the same length at dawn, noon and dusk. "As if," the youngest scholar says, and then does not finish, because the others are glaring at her.

choices.text: Leave the scholars to their books

effects.log: You have your own work. But for a while, whenever you face west, it feels a little like facing a door.

events.text: The magistrate posts a notice at the foot of the hill: by order of the county, the structure is closed and all approach forbidden. The next morning the notice board is found on the topmost step, set square before the doors. The notice has been folded neatly in four and weighed down with a pebble. On its back, in a small, old, careful hand, someone has written one word: "Already."

choices.text: Take the notice to the magistrate

effects.log: The magistrate reads the one word for a long time, then folds the notice again exactly as it was folded and puts it in a drawer. No new notice goes up.

choices.text: Keep the notice for yourself

effects.log: You keep it in your robe. The paper is ordinary paper. The hand is not like any hand you know, and yet it looks like it has written that word, to someone, many times.

choices.text: Put the board back and say nothing

effects.log: You carry it down the hill and set it up again. Nobody moves it a second time. It seems to have made its point.

events.text: No bird nests on the pagoda. Not a sparrow under its hundred eaves, not a crow on its rails. But every dawn the swallows of the whole town rise together from the rooftops, fly up the hill, circle it once, very high, around the highest roof, and come back down to their own business as if nothing had happened.

choices.text: Climb a roof at dawn to watch them go

effects.log: They pass so close you feel the wind of them. At the top of their circle, for one heartbeat, every bird is silent. Then they come home chattering, as though they had been asked something and answered it.

choices.text: Ask the bird-catcher why they do it

effects.log: The bird-catcher takes your coin and thinks. "Swallows go where there is going to be weather," he says. "I have never known them go where there was going to be a door."

choices.text: Let birds be birds

effects.log: You sleep through the dawns after that. When you do wake early, you find yourself counting the swallows anyway.

events.text: A merchant in the market is selling roof tiles "from the Hundred-Roofed Pagoda" at ten taels apiece. The tiles are ordinary clay. Everyone who has tried knows that the real ones cannot be chipped, cannot be lifted, and are always, even at midnight in winter, faintly warm.

choices.text: Expose him in front of the crowd

effects.log: You crack one of his tiles on your knee. The crowd laughs, the merchant flees, and an old woman thanks you so warmly you suspect she bought three.

choices.text: Buy one anyway, for the story

effects.log: It is a cold, ordinary tile, and you pay 10 taels for it. Months later you notice you keep it by your bed, and that you are a little disappointed, every night, that it is not warm.

choices.text: Go up and lay a hand on a real tile instead

effects.log: It is warm, as they say, and smooth, and under your palm you feel something very faint, very slow and very patient, like the pulse of someone asleep.

events.text: No one is on the hill tonight. You climb the steps alone, and your senses, which can hear a leaf land at a hundred paces, hear nothing at all from inside: no breath, no qi, no echo. Only the dust on the first step, and the doors. Up close the wood has the grain of something touched by a great many hands. You have opened sealed tombs and sect vaults. This is not like them. This feels like being looked at.

choices.text: Lay your palm flat on the door

effects.log: The wood is warm, like a cheek. For a long moment, nothing. Then something answers, not in your ears but under your breastbone, in a voice as dry and patient as an old broom on stone: "Not yet." The warmth goes out of the door. Your palm comes away dusty, and you find you do not want to wash it.

choices.text: Strike it with your full qi, as the sects did

effects.log: Your strike goes into the door and the door gives it back, gently, the way a hand rolls a ball back across a mat. Nothing answers. It was not knocked on that way.

choices.text: Bow to it, and go back down

effects.log: You bow as you would at an old master's grave and go back down the steps. Halfway, you have the feeling of having been noted.

events.text: You have never touched the pagoda's door in this life. But passing the foot of its hill on a cold evening, your right palm grows warm, as if it remembered for you, and for one breath you hear, or think you hear, a broom on stone, and a voice that once told you to wait.

choices.text: Climb up and lay your hand on the door again

effects.log: The door is warm. Nothing answers. You stand there until it is dark, and it seems to you that silence, here, is a kind of answer too: not yet, but not never.

choices.text: Call up the steps: "I have not forgotten."

effects.log: Your voice goes up the hundred roofs and does not come back. Then, high above, one bell at one eave stirs on a windless evening, and is still again.

choices.text: Walk on. It will keep

effects.log: You walk on. The warmth stays in your palm all the way home, like a coin someone pressed there and told you to keep safe.

events.text: Below the Jade Court the cloud sea lies white and unbroken, as it has lain for ten thousand years. This morning it is broken. Far off, something stands up through it: the tip of a spire, roof above roof, rising out of the clouds the way a mountain rises out of mist. Nothing from the mortal world reaches this high. The immortals at the railings have stopped talking.

choices.text: Fly out to it

effects.log: You fly until the Court is a speck behind you, and the spire is exactly as far away as it was when you set out. You turn back at dusk, and it is no nearer and no further, and somehow that feels like courtesy.

choices.text: Ask the old immortal beside you what it is

effects.log: "It came once before," the elder says, and then frowns, as if unsure where the words came from. "No. I do not know. I have never known. Is that not strange, for us?"

choices.text: Watch it from the railing until it fades

effects.log: By noon the clouds have closed over it. You find you have stood at the railing half a day without once thinking of your own cultivation, and that your qi has settled as if after a long sleep.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court lets you look through the great ledger, where every mountain, river and spirit under Heaven has its page and its ruling. One page has only a heading and nothing below it, not even a date. The heading reads: "The pagoda. Matters Heaven declines to rule on."

choices.text: Ask the clerk why Heaven declines

effects.log: The clerk looks round before answering. "Heaven does not decline," the clerk says. "Heaven was asked, and is still thinking. It has been thinking for a long time. Please do not write that down."

choices.text: Read the pages around it

effects.log: The page before is a river, the page after a mountain. Both are full of rulings in a dozen hands. Only this one is empty, and its paper is the oldest in the book.

choices.text: Close the ledger. Some pages should stay blank

effects.log: The clerk looks at you with sudden respect, and closes it gently, as if it might wake.

events.text: In the Upper Realm nothing from below is ever heard. Today, at noon, a bell is: one stroke, deep and plain, coming up through the clouds as if they were not there. The jade cups tremble on every table of the Court. An old immortal you have never once seen show feeling sets down a cup, goes out alone onto the terrace, and stands there until night, holding something small and dark in one closed hand.

choices.text: Go out and stand beside the old immortal

effects.log: The elder does not look at you. "When I was small," the elder says, "someone I loved cast bells." That is all. At nightfall the hand opens a little, and you glimpse old bronze, and then it closes again.

choices.text: Listen for a second stroke

effects.log: There is none. But for the rest of the day every immortal in the Court speaks a little more softly, as if somewhere below them a door were listening.

choices.text: Ask the Court's scholars where the sound came from

effects.log: They argue for a month and agree only that it came from below the clouds, and that nothing below the clouds should be able to do that.

events.text: Three immortal sects sent envoys down through the clouds to claim the spire for themselves. They came back up within a day, robes dusty to the knee, and none of them will say what happened. At a banquet, after a great deal of wine, one of them says only: "It does not open for a command." Then the envoy laughs, a little wildly, and leaves the table.

choices.text: Follow the envoy and ask what they saw

effects.log: "Steps," the envoy says. "And dust on the first one. And someone's broom leaning on the doorpost. Three sects of immortals, and nobody would touch the broom. Is that not funny?" It does not seem funny to either of you.

choices.text: Say aloud what everyone is thinking: then it opens for something else

effects.log: The banquet goes very quiet. A great elder looks at you along the table for a long moment, and then, very slightly, nods.

choices.text: Keep your counsel and your cup

effects.log: You hold your cup and say nothing, and later that night, alone, you go to the railing and look down at the clouds for a long time.
